subject: biology
unit_name: Structural Organisation in Animals and Plants
overview: This unit covers how flowering plants are built and how they vary in form: external morphology, tissues, internal anatomy, inflorescence, flowers, fruits, seeds and the diagnostic features of important families. It also covers how animal bodies are organised, from basic animal tissues to the complete body plan of the frog. NEET asks many direct, fact-based questions from here on examples, placentation, aestivation, floral formulae, tissue locations and frog organ systems, so precise NCERT-level recall scores easy marks.

topics.explanation: A flowering plant has an underground root system and an aerial shoot system made of stem, leaves, flowers and fruits. Root systems are of three kinds. Dicots have a tap root, monocots such as wheat have fibrous roots, and adventitious roots arise from parts other than the radicle, as in grass, Monstera and banyan. Roots, stems and leaves are often modified for storage, support, climbing, protection, respiration or vegetative propagation. The stem bears nodes and internodes, while the root never does. Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. Venation is the arrangement of veins in the lamina. It is usually reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots. A leaf may be simple, or compound with incisions reaching the midrib or petiole. Compound leaves are pinnate (neem) or palmate (silk cotton).
key_points: Root regions from tip upward: root cap, meristematic region, region of elongation, region of maturation (root hairs)
Storage roots: carrot (tap, conical), turnip (tap, napiform), sweet potato (adventitious, tuberous)
Prop roots occur in banyan; stilt roots in maize and sugarcane; pneumatophores in Rhizophora (mangrove)
Underground storage stems: potato (tuber), ginger and turmeric (rhizome), Colocasia and zaminkand (corm)
Stem tendrils (from axillary bud) occur in cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon and grapevine; stem thorns in Citrus and Bougainvillea
Flattened green photosynthetic stems: Opuntia (phylloclade) and Euphorbia
Subaerial stems: runner in grass and strawberry, stolon in mint and jasmine, offset in Pistia and Eichhornia, sucker in banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum
Leaf parts: leaf base, petiole, lamina; legumes have a swollen leaf base called pulvinus, and monocots have a sheathing leaf base
Phyllotaxy: alternate in China rose, mustard and sunflower; opposite in Calotropis and guava; whorled in Alstonia

Leaf modifications: tendrils in pea, spines in cactus, fleshy storage leaves in onion and garlic, phyllode (flattened petiole) in Australian Acacia, insect-trapping leaves in pitcher plant and Venus fly trap
topics.neet_tip: Expect example-matching questions such as modification type versus plant, and single-word definitions like phyllotaxy or venation.
topics.topic: Morphology and modifications of flowering plants

topics.explanation:
Plant tissues are either meristematic (dividing) or permanent (non-dividing).

Meristems are of three kinds:
- Apical meristems lie at root and shoot tips and cause primary growth in length.
- Intercalary meristems occur at the base of internodes, as in grasses.
- Lateral meristems, namely vascular cambium and cork cambium, cause secondary growth in girth.

Simple permanent tissues have one cell type:
- Parenchyma is thin-walled and does storage and photosynthesis.
- Collenchyma has walls thickened at the corners with cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin. It gives mechanical support to young dicot stems and petioles and is absent in monocots.
- Sclerenchyma has dead, lignified cells, either fibres or sclereids.

Complex permanent tissues are xylem and phloem:
- Xylem conducts water and minerals. It contains tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma.
- Phloem conducts food. It contains sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.

Plants have three tissue systems: epidermal, ground and vascular.
key_points: Tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are dead; xylem parenchyma is the only living xylem element
Vessels are characteristic of angiosperms; gymnosperms lack vessels
Protoxylem is formed first and metaxylem later
Xylem is exarch in roots (protoxylem towards the periphery) and endarch in stems (protoxylem towards the centre)
Mature sieve tube elements lack a nucleus and have perforated end walls called sieve plates; companion cells control them
Gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells instead of companion cells and sieve tubes
Phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocots; phloem fibres (bast fibres) are the only dead phloem cells
Epidermal tissue system includes epidermis, cuticle, stomata, trichomes and root hairs
Guard cells are bean-shaped in dicots and dumb-bell shaped in grasses; nearby specialised cells are subsidiary cells
Root hairs are unicellular; stem hairs (trichomes) are usually multicellular
Vascular bundles are radial in roots and conjoint in stems and leaves; they are open (with cambium) in dicot stems and closed in monocots
topics.neet_tip: NEET frequently asks which cells are living or dead, the components of xylem and phloem, and open versus closed or radial versus conjoint vascular bundles.

topics.explanation:
Roots: In a dicot root, the layers from outside inward are epiblema with root hairs, a parenchymatous cortex, and an endodermis whose cells carry suberised Casparian strips. Inside these lie the pericycle, 2 to 4 alternating xylem and phloem patches separated by conjunctive tissue, and a small pith. A monocot root has more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles and a large, well-developed pith, and it shows no secondary growth.

Stems: A dicot stem has a cuticle and epidermis, a collenchymatous hypodermis, a cortex, and an endodermis that acts as a starch sheath. The pericycle bears semilunar sclerenchyma patches. Vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral, open and endarch, arranged in a ring around a large pith, with medullary rays between them. A monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and numerous scattered vascular bundles. Each bundle is closed, enclosed in a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath and has a water-containing cavity.

Leaves: Dicot leaves are dorsiventral, with palisade mesophyll on the upper (adaxial) side and spongy mesophyll below. Monocot leaves are isobilateral.

Functions: roots absorb and anchor, stems conduct and support, and leaves photosynthesise and transpire.
key_points: Endodermis has Casparian strips of suberin, which block apoplastic water flow
Pericycle forms lateral roots and contributes to vascular cambium in dicot roots
Dicot root: diarch to tetrarch; monocot root: polyarch (more than 6)
Dicot stem bundles: conjoint, collateral, open, endarch, arranged in a ring
Monocot stem: scattered closed bundles, sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, no phloem parenchyma, peripheral bundles smaller
Ground tissue in monocot stem is not differentiated into cortex and pith
Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: more stomata on the abaxial (lower) surface
Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: stomata on both surfaces and undifferentiated mesophyll
Grass leaves have bulliform cells on the adaxial epidermis; they lose turgor in water stress and the leaf rolls to cut water loss
In leaves, xylem lies towards the adaxial side and phloem towards the abaxial side; bundle sheath cells surround the veins
topics.neet_tip: Questions usually present a transverse section feature (scattered bundles, polyarch xylem, bulliform cells, Casparian strip) and ask you to identify the organ or plant group.
topics.topic: Anatomy and functions of root, stem and leaf

topics.explanation: An inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis. It is decided by whether the shoot apex turns into a flower. In racemose inflorescence, the main axis keeps growing and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession: older flowers are at the base and younger ones towards the apex. In cymose inflorescence, the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited. Flowers then arise in basipetal order, with the oldest flower at the top or centre. Racemose types include raceme, spike, catkin, spadix, corymb, umbel and capitulum (head). Cymes are classified by the number of lateral branches formed below the terminal flower: monochasial (one), dichasial (two) or polychasial (many).
key_points: Racemose: indefinite growth of main axis, acropetal order, oldest flower at the base or periphery
Cymose: main axis ends in a flower, basipetal order, oldest flower at the apex or centre
Raceme (stalked flowers on a long axis): mustard
Spike (sessile flowers): Achyranthes
Catkin (pendulous spike of unisexual flowers): mulberry
Spadix (fleshy axis covered by a spathe): banana and Colocasia
Umbel (flowers arising from one point): coriander
Corymb (lower pedicels longer, flowers reach one level): candytuft (Iberis)
Capitulum or head (flattened receptacle with florets): sunflower and Tridax
Monochasial cymes are helicoid or scorpioid; dichasial cyme occurs in jasmine; polychasial cyme in Calotropis
topics.neet_tip: NEET tests the difference in growth of the main axis and flower order (acropetal versus basipetal), and matches inflorescence types with examples.

topics.explanation:
Flower: The flower is a modified shoot that carries out sexual reproduction. It has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
- Symmetry can be actinomorphic (radial), zygomorphic (bilateral) or asymmetric.
- Ovary position can be hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior) or epigynous (inferior ovary).
- Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud: valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary.
- Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary.

Fruit: The fruit is a mature ovary formed after fertilisation. A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic. The fruit wall (pericarp) may be differentiated into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp.

Seed: The seed is a fertilised ovule. It has a seed coat (outer testa and inner tegmen), a hilum, a micropyle and an embryo with radicle, plumule and one or two cotyledons. Seeds are endospermic or non-endospermic.
key_points: Actinomorphic flowers: mustard, datura, chilli; zygomorphic: pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia; asymmetric: canna
Hypogynous: mustard, China rose, brinjal; perigynous: plum, rose, peach; epigynous: guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower
Aestivation: valvate in Calotropis; twisted in China rose, lady's finger and cotton; imbricate in Cassia and gulmohur; vexillary in pea and bean
Stamen arrangements: epipetalous in brinjal, epiphyllous in lily, monadelphous in China rose, diadelphous in pea, polyadelphous in Citrus
Placentation: marginal in pea; axile in China rose, tomato and lemon; parietal in mustard and Argemone; free central in Dianthus and Primrose; basal in sunflower and marigold
Apocarpous gynoecium (free carpels): lotus, rose; syncarpous (fused carpels): mustard, tomato
Drupe: develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and is one-seeded, as in mango and coconut
In mango the edible part is the fleshy mesocarp; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous
Non-endospermic dicot seeds: bean, gram, pea; endospermic dicot seed: castor
Monocot (maize) seed is usually endospermic; it has an aleurone layer, a scutellum (single cotyledon), a coleoptile around the plumule and a coleorhiza around the radicle
topics.neet_tip: Placentation, aestivation and ovary-position match-the-list questions with example plants are among the most repeated in this unit.

topics.explanation:
Families are identified from vegetative, floral and fruit characters, summarised as floral formulae.

- Malvaceae (China rose, cotton, okra): epicalyx present, twisted corolla, numerous monadelphous stamens with monothecous (reniform) anthers, superior pentacarpellary syncarpous ovary with axile placentation.
- Cruciferae or Brassicaceae (mustard, radish, cabbage): cruciform corolla, tetradynamous stamens, bicarpellary ovary with parietal placentation and a false septum (replum). The fruit is a siliqua.
- Leguminosae (Fabaceae in the broad sense): bears legumes. Its subfamily Papilionoideae (pea, gram) has papilionaceous corolla with vexillary aestivation, diadelphous stamens and a monocarpellary ovary with marginal placentation.
- Compositae or Asteraceae (sunflower, marigold, Tridax): capitulum, pappus, syngenesious epipetalous stamens, inferior bicarpellary unilocular ovary with basal placentation. The fruit is a cypsela.
- Gramineae or Poaceae (wheat, rice, maize, bamboo): spikelets, lodicules, versatile anthers, feathery stigmas. The fruit is a caryopsis.
key_points: Malvaceae: epicalyx, gamosepalous valvate calyx, twisted polypetalous corolla, staminal tube, axile placentation, fruit capsule or schizocarp
Cruciferae: racemose (corymbose raceme) inflorescence, 4 free sepals in two whorls, 4 cruciform petals
Cruciferae: tetradynamous stamens (2 short outer and 4 long inner), parietal placentation with replum, fruit siliqua or silicula
Leguminosae has three subfamilies: Papilionoideae, Caesalpinioideae and Mimosoideae
Papilionoideae corolla: 1 standard (vexillum), 2 wings (alae) and 2 fused keel petals (carina)
Papilionoideae: stamens diadelphous (9)+1; legumes have root nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria and pulvinate leaves
Caesalpinioideae (Cassia, Tamarindus, gulmohur): imbricate (ascending) aestivation and zygomorphic flowers
Mimosoideae (Mimosa, Acacia): actinomorphic flowers, valvate aestivation, numerous stamens, often head inflorescence
Compositae: outer ray florets are ligulate, zygomorphic and often female or neuter; inner disc florets are tubular, actinomorphic and bisexual
Compositae: calyx reduced to pappus (aids wind dispersal), anthers fused but filaments free (syngenesious), single ovule per ovary
Gramineae: hollow (fistular) internodes, leaf sheath with ligule, fibrous roots, parallel venation
Gramineae: each floret is enclosed by lemma and palea, perianth reduced to 2 or 3 lodicules, stamens usually 3 (6 in rice and bamboo), monocarpellary superior ovary with one basal ovule
Gramineae fruit is a caryopsis, in which the pericarp is fused with the seed coat

formulas.meaning: Malvaceae (China rose): actinomorphic, bisexual, epicalyx, gamosepalous calyx, free petals, numerous monadelphous stamens, superior syncarpous pentacarpellary ovary
Cruciferae (mustard): 4 sepals in two whorls, 4 cruciform petals, tetradynamous stamens, superior bicarpellary syncarpous ovary
Leguminosae, Papilionoideae (pea): zygomorphic, papilionaceous corolla, diadelphous stamens, superior monocarpellary ovary
Compositae disc floret (sunflower): calyx as pappus, gamopetalous corolla, 5 epipetalous syngenesious stamens, inferior bicarpellary ovary
Gramineae (wheat): perianth reduced to lodicules, 3 stamens with versatile anthers, superior ovary with one ovule
A line below G means superior ovary (hypogynous); a line above G means inferior ovary (epigynous); brackets mean fusion

topics.neet_tip: NEET gives statements on stamen condition, placentation, ovary position or fruit type and asks which family they fit, so learn the floral formula of each family.
topics.topic: Families: Malvaceae, Cruciferae, Leguminosae, Compositae and Gramineae

topics.explanation:
Animal tissues are of four basic types.

1. Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines cavities, with little intercellular matrix. Simple epithelium can be squamous, cuboidal, columnar or ciliated. Compound epithelium is multilayered and protective. Glandular epithelium may be unicellular or multicellular, and exocrine or endocrine.
2. Connective tissue links and supports other tissues. It includes loose connective tissue (areolar, adipose), dense connective tissue (regular, irregular) and specialised connective tissue (cartilage, bone, blood). Except blood, these cells secrete collagen or elastin fibres.
3. Muscle tissue can be skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (fusiform, non-striated, involuntary) or cardiac (striated, branched, involuntary, with intercalated discs).
4. Neural tissue consists of neurons, which are excitable, and neuroglia, which support and protect neurons.
key_points: Simple squamous epithelium: walls of blood vessels and air sacs (alveoli) of lungs
Simple cuboidal epithelium: ducts of glands and tubular parts of nephrons; PCT has a brush border of microvilli
Simple columnar epithelium: lining of stomach and intestine; it may bear microvilli
Ciliated epithelium: bronchioles and fallopian tubes
Compound epithelium: dry surface of skin, moist surface of buccal cavity and pharynx, inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and pancreatic ducts
Goblet cells are unicellular glands; salivary glands are multicellular; exocrine glands secrete through ducts, endocrine glands release hormones directly into fluid
Cell junctions: tight junctions stop leakage, adhering junctions cement cells, gap junctions allow passage of ions and small molecules
Adipose tissue stores fat; tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments attach bone to bone (dense regular); skin dermis is dense irregular
Cartilage cells (chondrocytes) and bone cells (osteocytes) lie in lacunae; bone matrix is rich in calcium salts and collagen fibres
Cardiac muscle cells are joined by intercalated discs, which let them contract as a unit
Neuroglia make up more than one-half the volume of neural tissue
topics.neet_tip: Expect location-of-tissue match questions (which epithelium lines what, tendon versus ligament) and statement questions on cell junctions and muscle types.

topics.explanation:
The common Indian frog is Rana tigrina, now called Hoplobatrachus tigerinus. Frogs are cold-blooded (poikilothermic) and escape extreme heat and cold by aestivation and hibernation. Their body has a head and trunk but no neck or tail. The skin is moist, mucus-covered and absorbs water, so frogs do not drink water.
- Respiration: in water, frogs breathe through the skin (cutaneous respiration). On land, they use the buccal cavity, skin and lungs.
- Circulation: closed, with a three-chambered heart (2 atria, 1 ventricle), plus hepatic portal and renal portal systems.
- Excretion: frogs are ureotelic.
- Nervous system: the brain is divided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, and 10 pairs of cranial nerves arise from it.
- Reproduction: sexes are separate. Fertilisation is external in water, and development is indirect through a tadpole larva that undergoes metamorphosis.
key_points: Eyes have a nictitating membrane; a tympanum receives sound; frogs have no external ear
Forelimbs have 4 digits; hindlimbs have 5 webbed digits for swimming
Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb
Digestive system: short alimentary canal (carnivorous), bilobed tongue free in front, maxillary and vomerine teeth, opening into the cloaca
Liver bile is stored in the gall bladder; digestion occurs in the stomach (HCl, gastric juice) and intestine; absorption through villi and microvilli
Lungs are a pair of elongated pink sac-like structures; during aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange is through the skin
Heart: sinus venosus opens into the right atrium, and the conus arteriosus arises from the ventricle on the ventral side
RBCs are nucleated; blood has plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets; a lymphatic system is present
Forebrain: olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon; midbrain: a pair of optic lobes; hindbrain: cerebellum and medulla oblongata
Sense organs: touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (simple eyes), hearing (tympanum with internal ears)
Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads
Male: yellowish ovoid testes attached to the kidneys by mesorchium; 10 to 12 vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal, which joins the urinogenital duct
Female: ovaries have no functional connection with the kidneys; oviducts open into the cloaca; 2500 to 3000 ova are laid at a time
Ecological role: frogs eat insects and protect crops; frog legs are used as food in some countries
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks direct one-liners on the mode of respiration in water versus on land, the number of cranial nerves, heart chambers, and the male versus female urinogenital arrangement.
topics.topic: Frog: morphology, anatomy and organ systems (digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, reproductive)

key_facts: Frogs respire through the skin in water and through the buccal cavity, skin and lungs on land.
Frogs have 10 pairs of cranial nerves.
Frog heart has three chambers: two atria and one ventricle, with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus.
Frogs are ureotelic; in males the ureter acts as a urinogenital duct, while in females the ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca.
A female frog lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time; fertilisation is external.
Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves: alternate in China rose, opposite in Calotropis and guava, whorled in Alstonia.
Placentation: marginal in pea, axile in tomato and China rose, parietal in mustard and Argemone, free central in Dianthus and Primrose, basal in sunflower and marigold.
Twisted aestivation occurs in China rose, lady's finger and cotton; vexillary aestivation occurs in pea and bean.
Monadelphous stamens occur in China rose, diadelphous in pea, polyadelphous in Citrus.
Cruciferae has tetradynamous stamens, a siliqua fruit and a replum.
Compositae has syngenesious stamens, a pappus, an inferior ovary with basal placentation and a cypsela fruit.
Gramineae has lodicules, versatile anthers, a caryopsis fruit and hollow internodes.
Malvaceae has an epicalyx, monadelphous stamens and monothecous (reniform) anthers.
Potato is a stem tuber; sweet potato is a modified adventitious root.
Stilt roots occur in maize and sugarcane, prop roots in banyan, pneumatophores in Rhizophora.
Phylloclade occurs in Opuntia; phyllode occurs in Australian Acacia.
Dicot root has 2 to 4 xylem bundles (diarch to tetrarch); monocot root has more than 6 (polyarch).
Casparian strips in the endodermis are made of suberin.
Vascular bundles are open in dicot stems and closed in monocot stems, with protoxylem cavities in monocots.
Bulliform cells in grass leaves cause leaf rolling under water stress.
Collenchyma is absent in monocots; vessels are absent in gymnosperms.
Mature sieve tube elements lack a nucleus and are controlled by companion cells.
Simple squamous epithelium lines blood vessels and lung alveoli; ciliated epithelium lines bronchioles and fallopian tubes.
Tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone; both are dense regular connective tissue.
Intercalated discs are found only in cardiac muscle.
In mango the edible part is the mesocarp; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous.
Castor seed is endospermic; bean, gram and pea seeds are non-endospermic.
common_traps: Saying frogs breathe through lungs in water. In water, respiration is cutaneous (through the skin); lungs are used on land.
Confusing frog cranial nerves (10 pairs) with human cranial nerves (12 pairs).
Treating potato, ginger and Colocasia as roots. They are underground stems because they bear nodes and buds; sweet potato and carrot are roots.
Mixing up parietal (Argemone, mustard) with free central (Primrose, Dianthus) placentation. Free central has ovules on a central axis without septa.
Confusing syngenesious stamens (anthers fused, filaments free, in Compositae) with monadelphous stamens (filaments fused into one bundle, in Malvaceae).
Assuming a line above G means superior ovary. A line below G means superior; a line above G means inferior, as in Compositae.
Thinking monocot stems have open bundles and secondary growth. Monocot bundles are closed and scattered, so there is normally no secondary growth.
Thinking the racemose oldest flower is at the top. In racemose, flowers are acropetal, so the oldest is at the base; in cymose the terminal flower is the oldest.
quick_revision: Racemose inflorescence: main axis keeps growing, acropetal order. Cymose: axis ends in a flower, basipetal order.
Placentation: pea marginal, tomato axile, Argemone parietal, Primrose free central, sunflower basal.
Aestivation: Calotropis valvate, China rose twisted, Cassia imbricate, pea vexillary.
Cruciferae floral formula is K 2+2, C4, A 2+4, G(2) superior; fruit siliqua.
Papilionoideae floral formula is K(5), C 1+2+(2), A (9)+1, G1 superior; fruit legume.
Malvaceae has epicalyx and monadelphous stamens; Compositae has pappus, syngenesious stamens and cypsela; Gramineae has lodicules and caryopsis.
Dicot root is diarch to tetrarch; monocot root is polyarch with a large pith.
Dicot stem bundles are in a ring, open; monocot stem bundles are scattered, closed, with a bundle sheath.
Dicot leaf is dorsiventral; grass leaf is isobilateral with bulliform cells.
Squamous epithelium lines alveoli and vessels; cuboidal lines PCT and gland ducts; columnar lines gut; ciliated lines bronchioles and fallopian tube.
Frog: skin breathing in water, 3-chambered heart, 10 pairs of cranial nerves, ureotelic, external fertilisation, tadpole stage.
Male frog has vocal sacs, a copulatory pad, and Bidder's canal linking testes to the urinogenital duct.
